title: Two friends at the festival
hook: Upatissa and Kolita watch a festival and suddenly find it empty

segments.voice: Yesterday: the poem, closed, the whole life told once more, and your line, the life, retold. Today a new block begins: the great disciples, the people who followed him.

Same seats as last year. Same hill above the city. Same crowd, same plays, same music, same jokes landing in the same places. Two young men from good families sit side by side in the best seats, as they always do at this festival. Other years, they laughed at the funny parts, cried at the sad ones and threw gifts to the performers. This year, the jokes land, and neither of them laughs. The sad scene plays, and neither of them cries. Each glances over and sees the other has gone quiet too.
screen: `SAME SEATS, SAME HILL.` → `THE JOKES LAND, NOBODY LAUGHS.` → `BOTH OF THEM, QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the two friends. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita. The commentaries say they were sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha, close friends since childhood, each with a circle of young companions around him. Later they'll be known by other names, Sariputta and Moggallana. But not yet. Right now they're two well-off young men at a festival. Second, the silence. The commentary tells it simply. Kolita turns to his friend: you don't seem to be enjoying yourself today. What's wrong? And Upatissa answers with a question of his own: what is there to look at here? Before long, all these people, the actors, the crowd, the two of them, will be gone. And here we sit, laughing. Third, the turn. Kolita has been thinking the same thing. Neither talked the other into it. They arrived at the same emptiness, in the same seats, on the same afternoon. Nothing about the festival was worse. What had changed was them. Fourth, the question that's left. They don't stay sad, and they don't go home and pretend. They decide, together, to look for a way out of birth and death, a release the festival can't give. Notice how close this sits to the prince's own story. He saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and the palace music went flat. These two never leave their seats. The emptiness finds them in the middle of the fun.
screen: `UPATISSA AND KOLITA.` · `WHAT IS THERE TO LOOK AT?` · `BOTH THINKING THE SAME THING.` · `A WAY OUT, NOT A WAY HOME.` · then, large: `THE SHOW WAS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Remember a moment when something meant to be fun went flat, a party, a show, a holiday you'd waited for, and recall the feeling honestly, without judging or fixing it. Ask what you were hungry for that the fun couldn't give, and let the question rest, unanswered, with the breath.
Upatissa. One of two friends who sit through the festival they loved and find it suddenly empty, with his friend Kolita feeling the same. Today's word.
Your line: the show was empty. Two friends, one feeling, and a search about to begin. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples; in some Theravada temples images of the two stand on either side of the Buddha, and their story is told in sermons and at festivals.

chat.says: Why would two friends suddenly stop enjoying a festival they loved?
options: Nothing was worse; they saw everyone there would soon be gone, and it felt empty.
The festival was badly run that year, so they left feeling cheated.
One friend was sad, and the other felt guilty and kept him company.
chat.meaning: Upatissa asked what there was to look at, since all of them would soon be gone. Kolita felt the same; what had changed was them.

Upatissa.meaning: a young man later known as Sariputta

Kolita.meaning: Upatissa's friend, later known as Moggallana

Rajagaha.meaning: a city ringed by hills, where the festival was held

Sariputta.meaning: one of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Moggallana.meaning: the other of the Buddha's two chief disciples

sources.ref: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada Atthakatha) on verses 11–12, the story of Sariputta and Moggallana

notes: All material paraphrased (Burlingame's Buddhist Legends, 1921, is not on the validator list).

Confirm the festival details in the Dhammapada commentary (and the parallel in the Anguttara/Theragatha commentaries): the hilltop festival at Rajagaha (Giragga), their laughing, weeping and giving gifts in earlier years, this year's silence, Kolita's question, Upatissa's answer. The commentary's answer includes a span of years ('within a hundred years'); the script says 'before long' to avoid a number.
'Close friends since childhood' and 'sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha' follow the commentary; tradition also says they were born on the same day (not used).
Comparison with the prince's sights is internal to the tradition (no other path compared).
howItsDone: the two chief disciples flanking the Buddha in Theravada temples; confirm.
Editor: Sariputta and Moggallana are the names the discourses use, so 'later tradition knows them' became 'later they'll be known'; howItsDone 'often' softened to 'in some'.

Audit: 'these two don't need a road trip' (a quip about the prince's chariot rides) made 'these two never leave their seats'; unclear 'neither of them dragged the other there' made 'talked the other into it'.
